items.stem: Students drop a course when they study very little and when they take on far too many other commitments. The students in the middle stay. Why can a single straight line not separate the stayers from the dropouts?

options.text: A line makes only two sides, and the stayers have dropouts on both sides of them.
options.feedback: Whichever way you angle one line, some stayers end up on the same side as dropouts.

options.text: There are too few students in the data to place a line between the groups.
options.feedback: The number of students is not the issue. The shape of the groups is.

options.text: The line has not been trained for long enough to find the right angle.
options.feedback: More training cannot fix a limit in the shape of a straight line.

options.text: Attendance matters more than hours studied, so one line cannot weigh both.
options.feedback: Which measurement matters more does not change the fact that the stayers are surrounded.

items.stem: A network has its nonlinearity switched off, and the number of units goes from 2 to 8. What happens to the accuracy?

options.text: It stays flat. Adding straight lines together gives another straight line.
options.feedback: Without the nonlinearity, the layer can only add its units, and the sum of straight lines is a straight line. More units give no new shape.

options.text: It rises to 100 percent as units are added, because more lines fit better.
options.feedback: That happens only when the nonlinearity is on. Switched off, the units cannot combine into a curve.

options.text: It rises a little with each unit, because each line cuts off a few more students.
options.feedback: Each extra unit adds nothing new when the nonlinearity is off.

options.text: It falls to zero, because the lines cancel each other out completely.
options.feedback: The network still draws a straight line, so some students are classified correctly.

items.stem: A neural network for the dropout problem has four units in its hidden layer. What does each unit correspond to on the plot of students?

options.text: One straight line, set by that unit's weights and bias
options.feedback: A unit is one line. Its two input weights set the angle and its bias sets how far out it sits.

options.text: One student in the data, shown as a point on the plot
options.feedback: Students are the points on the plot. The circles in the diagram are units.

options.text: One of the four regions of the plot where students stay
options.feedback: The stay region is the overlap of all the lines. It is not assigned to one unit.

options.text: One of the measurements a person chose to feed into the network
options.feedback: The measurements are the inputs to the network. The hidden units are set up by the network itself.

items.stem: A bank uses a deep learning model to score loan applications. The model is very accurate, but a regulator asks which measurements drove a particular rejection. Why is that hard to answer?

options.text: It builds its own features inside hidden layers, and no single number there has a plain meaning.
options.feedback: With hand-picked features you could point at the one that was wrong. In a deep network, billions of numbers combine and none of them means anything alone.

options.text: Deep learning models are always less accurate than simple ones, so the question has no good answer.
options.feedback: Deep models are often more accurate. The difficulty is explaining them.

options.text: The bank did not keep the applicant's data, so there is nothing to examine.
options.feedback: Having the data does not explain what the hidden layers did with it.

options.text: The output unit does not produce an answer for rejected applications.
options.feedback: The output unit does produce an answer. The hidden units that fed it are hard to interpret.
